comments.author: imtringued
comments.text:
I keep getting clickbait youtube videos about how "NCM" obsoletes "LLMs" and "Nvidia memory chips" (yes, it's that bad).
This makes me wonder what these people think an "LLM" even is. The name itself implies that it is large and about language. It does not imply that an "LLM" is inherently autoregressive or that it has any particular architecture  even though most LLMs are transformers. Anything can be a large language model as long as it is large and models language.
NCM is basically a hierarchical diffusion transformer where the further layers take one big token and then generate two smaller tokens. So it is more like an evaluation strategy. You could apply this to any model architecture.
I personally think the name NCM itself is terrible because it contains the word "next" which inherently implies an ordering and somehow we are supposed to think that "LLM" which contains no mention of ordering, is constrained to ordered token production.

Paper here:

Like, sure, they can take screenshots of a few snapshotted states, but in terms of how things react as underlying nodes move and (potentially) reflow. correct

right
, and the code you write is about as minimal as you can get - though the paper notes that state management is somewhat complex. But this seems solvable!
Once this is ported to HTML, it'll become an incredible part of t

comments.author: tablatom
comments.text:
Imagine an agentic coding system with a good memory implementation. It's prompted to build an app with sophisticated drag-and-drop features. And then another one... After twenty such apps it realises there must be better way and comes up with declarative dragging.

comments.author: SkiFire13
comments.text:
In my opinion this comes down to how much data you have on screen and whether you can efficiently skip off-screen data. If you can do that then it doesn't matter how your framework scales, you will be bound by screen space anyway.
That said, I indeed am not fond of GPUI and egui, but for different reasons.
In GPUI having to manually mark the state as changed is IMO a footgun and any decent UI framework should not require something like that.
In egui I found the "immediate mutation" pattern (e.g. the classic `if button.pressed() { mutate }`) to produce glitches in the UI, because it will cause half the UI to draw the old state and half the new state. You almost always want to anticipate interactions, or to delay mutations. But performance is not a problem IMO unless you're writing a complex vector graphics viewport (in which case retained UI won't help you either)

When I had started my PhD, I thought the writing part of a paper was just the last thing I needed to do to summarize my results, like a boring epilogue to the more exciting science. And to be able to do that you need clarity of mind, you need to have worked through multiple drafts to be able to get to your point as efficiently and clearly as possible. actually
researching during the writing part.
The problem with AI writing is that it makes people believe that writing is just writing and not a tool for thinking very deeply about the topic you are writing about. I am not completely opposed to AI assisted writing, but if I see AI writing, it’s telling me that the author tried to take a shortcut in their own thinking and it’s a good heuristic that the ideas will not be thought through enough to warrant my complete attention.

comments.text:

But, to the claim of how to think in the age of LLMs, I think it’s worth contrasting the other approach, which is a dialog with the LLM; two things are needed IMO to keep things honest:
First, you need to keep asking the LLM to explain things, until you understand what it did. Lots of angles here; have the LLM make a design/product doc, write one-off architecture explainers, write throwaway data-viz tools to explain the data distribution. Then ask a fresh copy to adversarially review the core concepts. Try asking a different frontier model too.
Second, you need to push for “proof”, in other words, ask for demos and try it yourself. Imagine yourself a CEO or VC; how do you know if the output of an entire org is vaporware? One thing to beware is launching into a field where you don’t have expertise and can’t actually validate the output.
